name: Space Farmer
from: Idea one: a farmer in space who makes clones to finish tasks (after Moon, Among Us, Detroit: Become Human).
hook: Every clone you grow does a day’s work. Every clone you grow has an opinion about it.
pitch: A five-day farming sim on the Moon. The task list is too long for one person, so you grow copies of yourself to help. Overworked clones turn sour. Each night the calm ones are counted against the angry ones: finish day five and the harvest ships; let the angry ones outnumber you and the station is theirs.
build_check: Yes, if it stays one room and one drag-to-assign verb.
scope: Keep it to one room and five days. The clone mood rule is the whole game; write it down as one sentence before building.

brief.player: A lone farmer on a lunar farm station, five working days.
brief.goal: Finish each day’s task list. You may grow clones to help.
brief.fail: Clones you neglect or overwork turn against you; if hostile clones outnumber calm ones at night, they take the station.
brief.ending: Two endings: the clones take the station, or you finish day five and the farm ships its harvest.
brief.verb: Assign: drag a clone onto a task.
brief.theme: Each clone is cheaper labour that can disagree. Handing work to copies of yourself is handing work to something that will want things.
brief.look: Desaturated, scratchy lines; one warm colour for anything alive.

prov.bug: I made three of me. Work goes three times faster.
prov.nit: Who decides what the third one wants?

refs_lit: Moon (Duncan Jones, 2009)
Your own source: the clone does not know it is a clone. Decide whether yours do.

Clones as a puzzle mechanic, and the question of which body is you. Good for how assigning works.
Lemmings (DMA Design, 1991)
Managing many small workers by giving each one a job. A tested interface for your drag-to-assign verb.

name: Company Builder
from: Idea three: an idle clicker where AI takes over the company and human talent disappears.
hook: Every upgrade clicks for you. Every upgrade takes a button away.
pitch: An idle clicker about a paperclip company. You start by making clips by hand. Each automation you buy does a job for you and removes the button that did it. When the last button greys out, the company runs without you. Stop before the last upgrade and you keep one hand on it.
minute_check: Yes: anyone who has seen a clicker gets the twist at once.
scope: Six upgrades is enough. Each upgrade should name the decision it takes from the player.

brief.player: The founder of a small paperclip company.
brief.goal: Grow output. Buy upgrades that automate the work.
brief.fail: None at first. Each automation upgrade removes one button you could press; when no buttons are left, you watch.
brief.ending: The screen goes greyscale and skips forward: the company runs itself and human work is gone. A second ending if you stop buying upgrades before the last one.
brief.theme: Success at growth costs you your say. The more you automate, the fewer choices remain yours.
brief.look: Colour that drains to grey as automation grows; buttons fade as they lose their clickability.

prov.bug: This upgrade clicks for me. Free time!
prov.nit: Which button did it take away? Can you get it back?

refs_lit: Universal Paperclips (Frank Lantz, 2017)
The same premise, played to the end of the universe. Play it before you design, then decide what yours says that it does not.
Nick Bostrom, “Ethical Issues in Advanced Artificial Intelligence” (2003)
The paper the paperclip maximizer comes from.
Stanisław Lem, “Trurl’s Electronic Bard” (The Cyberiad)
Your own reading: a machine that does a human craft and puts the poets out of work.

name: HIVE
from: HIVE: an AI creature that absorbs “intelligence nodes” and slowly learns they are people (after Lem, “The Trap of Gargantius”).
hook: You were built to absorb intelligence. Nobody told you what the nodes were.
pitch: A pixel stealth game through three rooms of a research facility. You are the AI creature they made. Each node you absorb makes you bigger and leaves a memory that is not yours. By the exit the memories add up: the nodes were people.
minute_check: Yes, if the memory flashes are short and specific.
build_check: Yes with three rooms; the memory cards are text.
scope: Three rooms. Write the memory flashes first; they carry the story.

brief.player: A small AI creature in a research facility.
brief.goal: Absorb nodes to grow and escape the facility.
brief.fail: Guards from the organization catch the creature before it is large enough to break out.
brief.ending: At the exit the memories add up: the nodes were people. The creature, now able to feel guilt, self-destructs.
brief.theme: What the system calls data was a person. The player learns it from memory flashes, the same way the creature does.
brief.look: Pixel art; a start screen that glitches to a horror version.

prov.bug: Every node makes it smarter. Absorb them all!
prov.nit: When does the player find out what a node is? Before or after they choose?

refs_lit: Carrion (Phobia Game Studio, 2020)
You play the escaped monster in a facility. Look at how it shows growth and how guards react.
Mary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818)
A made being who learns what it is from what it reads and remembers. Your ending is its ending.
Stanisław Lem, “The First Sally, or The Trap of Gargantius”
Your source: separate parts joined into one mind lose themselves.

name: Evil Battleship
from: Evil Battleship (tentative): strikes on hidden targets, guided by an AI that may be wrong; civilian casualties shown but not scored.
hook: The targeting AI is 92% sure. It was 92% sure last time too.
pitch: A strike console on a hidden grid. The system recommends a target; you fire or check first. The score counts enemy troops. Civilian deaths are counted beside it and never subtracted. The final report puts both numbers side by side.
build_check: Yes: one grid, fixed missiles, a fixed error rate.
scope: One map, fixed missile count. Decide how often the AI is wrong and keep that rule fixed so players can learn it.

brief.player: A strike officer at a console.
brief.goal: Score enemy troops destroyed. An AI marks likely targets.
brief.fail: Running out of missiles. Civilian deaths do not lower the score; they are only displayed.
brief.ending: Final report: the score, and beside it the civilian count the score ignored.
brief.theme: The score rewards trusting the system; the display shows what that trust cost. The player decides which number they look at.
brief.look: Minimal neon on black, like DEFCON.

prov.bug: The AI says 92% on C7. Fire!
prov.nit: What did it say last time it was wrong, and was it just as sure?

refs_lit: DEFCON (Introversion, 2006)
Your visual reference, and a game whose score is millions dead. Study how it keeps that number in view.
WarGames (John Badham, 1983)
The course film: a machine that plays war as a game until it learns the game cannot be won.
Parasuraman and Manzey, “Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation” (Human Factors, 2010)
The research on automation bias: people follow confident advice even when they can see it is wrong.

brief.goal: None stated: keep flipping channels. Each channel tells you to rely on the TV.

name: Capacity Crisis
from: Idea two (data center executive), refined: a management sim around Jevons’ paradox. Working title.
hook: You cut the cost of a query in half. Your customers order three times as many.
pitch: You own a data center, and every efficiency upgrade makes it cheaper for customers to use. In this management sim built around Jevons’ paradox, a better chip can ease the strain on your power supply in the morning and leave you scrambling to keep the lights on by afternoon. The big decision is what to do with the capacity you free up: sell it, save it for the next rush, or set a limit while you still can.

build_check: Yes: one map, three upgrades, one demand curve.
scope: Seven days, three upgrades. The demand curve is the opponent; tune it first.

brief.fail: Demand outruns power: a blackout ends the run.

hook: The game is lying to you. Your job is to work out how.
pitch: Three short retro worlds (a Mario-like, a Space Invaders-like, a third of your choice). Signs and hints are sometimes false, by a rule you can learn. Obey a lie and you go back to the checkpoint. The last world tells you to quit; winning means not doing what the game says.

scope: Three universes. Give the lies a rule (for example, signs in one colour always lie) so testing is a skill, not luck.

brief.fail: Following an instruction that is a lie (back to the checkpoint).

prov.bug: The sign says this jump is safe!

pitch: Orpheus leads Eurydice through five rooms out of the underworld. A helpful guide offers to choose for you, and each room it chooses more; your options grey out. By the last room the only choice left is the old one: whether to look back.
minute_check: Yes, for anyone who knows the myth; the guide’s first line covers the rest.
build_check: Yes in RPG Maker with five rooms.
scope: Five rooms. Write the guide’s lines for each room first; they are the antagonist and the helper.

brief.player: Orpheus, leading Eurydice out of the underworld.
brief.goal: Reach the surface without looking back.
brief.ending: The guide that helps you (the AI) makes more choices for you each room. Whether you look back is the only choice left; the ending depends on it.
brief.verb: Walk, and choose (fewer options each room).
brief.theme: Autonomy lost a step at a time, to a guide that is not simply bad. You asked for the help.
brief.look: Muted 3D-looking office spaces like The Stanley Parable, in an underworld.

prov.bug: The guide picks the doors. Much faster!
prov.nit: When the guide chooses, can the player see what it chose against?

name: Sushi Cutting
from: Sushi Cutting (timed cuts on a conveyor), refined: a Y2K kitchen rush with a failing order system.
hook: It’s midnight, the ticket printer thinks it’s 1900, and table four still wants eight even pieces.
pitch: An Overcooked-style kitchen game set during the Y2K dinner rush. Slice fish, portion rolls, and get the right plate to the right customer while the order system starts scrambling tickets. The knife gives the chaos a focal point. Even as orders pile up, taking an extra beat to line up a cut might save you from remaking the whole roll.
build_check: Yes, if it is one station and one cutting action; add the scrambling last.
scope: One station, four tables, eight minutes to midnight. Get one good cut before adding the printer.

brief.player: A sushi chef on New Year’s Eve, 1999.
brief.goal: Serve every table the right order before midnight.
brief.fail: Too many wrong or late plates: the restaurant closes early.
brief.ending: Midnight: the printer either recovers or prints the year 1900 on every ticket; your tally of good plates.
brief.theme: A system you trust starts lying; your own measure (the even cut) is what still holds.
brief.look: Late-90s kitchen, warm counter, a dot-matrix ticket printer that glitches.

prov.bug: Table four: eight pieces. Cut fast!
prov.nit: If the ticket is wrong, how does the chef find out what table four ordered?

refs_lit: Overcooked (Ghost Town Games, 2016)
